content_voiceover: This question surveys novel agents approved for ALL, asking which description is wrong, and the answer is B. Clofarabine is indeed a deoxyadenosine analog, but it's FDA-approved specifically for pediatric and young adult patients, ages one to twenty-one, with relapsed or refractory ALL, not for adult patients as this statement claims, that's the error. The other statements are accurate, nelarabine is approved for relapsed or refractory T-cell ALL or T-lymphoblastic lymphoma, inotuzumab ozogamicin, a CD22-targeted antibody-drug conjugate linked to calicheamicin, is approved for CD22-positive relapsed or refractory precursor B-ALL, blinatumomab monotherapy showed longer survival than standard chemotherapy in relapsed or refractory ALL, and adding rituximab to standard chemo improved event-free survival specifically in CD20-positive ALL. The pattern across these novel-agent questions is knowing which drug targets which antigen, and which specific age or biomarker subgroup each approval applies to.
keypoints: Clofarabine: FDA approved only for pediatric/young adult (1-21y) R/R ALL, NOT adults
Nelarabine: for relapsed/refractory T-ALL or T-lymphoblastic lymphoma
Inotuzumab ozogamicin: anti-CD22 ADC for CD22+ precursor B-ALL
Rituximab added to chemo helps only in CD20-positive ALL
keypoint_voiceover: Match each novel agent to its exact approval, nelarabine for T-ALL, inotuzumab for CD22-positive B-ALL, blinatumomab as CD19/CD3 monotherapy, and rituximab only adds benefit in CD20-positive disease. The trap here is clofarabine, it's approved for pediatric and young adult relapsed ALL, not adults.
